power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Rapid technological innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed not only the resolution at which the brain can be observed, but also the questions that can be asked, shifting the field from description toward prediction, regulation and generation.
Yet progress has largely advanced along parallel trajectories, and findings at one level rarely inform or constrain the next.
Here, we review recent advances in three exemplary domains and propose a futureoriented framework for their integration.

First, molecular and cellular neurotechnology, including synaptic proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution microscopy, optoacoustic and ultrasound imaging, sonogenetics and molecular MRI, resolves neural processes with unprecedented specificity.

Second, AI-based decoding of human brain activity yields precise signatures of complex, subjective conscious experiences in naturalistic contexts and is beginning to inform diagnosis, drug evaluation and individualized neuromodulation in mental disorders.
Third, large-scale neural recordings, mechanistic whole-brain simulations, neural foundation models and AI surrogate brains are converging toward individualized digital twin brains.

We argue that the next level of progress requires integrating these domains into a closed loop of reciprocal constraints, in which molecular measurements inform model parameters, human signatures define and evaluate what models must reproduce, and model predictions prioritize perturbations that can be tested across domains.
Neuroscience has re-entered a phase of exceptional momentum.

Over the past decade, the convergence of advanced neuroimaging, molecular and electrophysiological neurotechnology, and artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically changed the resolution at which the brain can be observed.

Consequently, it has also changed the kind of question that can be asked: from describing pathways and localizing isolated functions, to building precise, individualized -and in part generative -models of how neural systems produce and regulate behavior, cognition and subjective experience.

Considerable advances have been made in elucidating how neural circuits give rise to behavior, how emerging technologies can read out, regulate or computationally model these circuits, and how their dysregulation contributes to devastating neurological and mental conditions.

Progress now spans biological and computational scales that were long treated in isolation, from ion channels and synaptic signaling in defined cell types and circuits, through the precise decoding of conscious cognitive and affective processes in humans, to in silico whole-brain generative simulations and AI-powered digital twin brains.

Across these fields, the ambition has shifted rapidly from description to prediction, observation to regulation, simulation to generation, ultimately paving the way to accelerate translation and application.
Two parallel global developments make this shift urgent and extend well beyond scientific interest alone.
The first is the rising health and socio-economic burden of brain-based conditions, as also emphasized in the World Health Organization (WHO) position paper on brain health [1].

text.text: Critically, the dominant cost driver for these conditions is not direct medical intervention, but lost labor-force participation or long-term social care.
This reflects that the currently available interventions lack sufficient efficacy or accessibility for substantial proportion of those affected.
The second development is the intense investment and capitalization of brain science and braininspired technology.

Large-scale public programmes, e.g. the U. However, as we now measure or simulate the brain across an extraordinary range of scales and with unprecedented precision, the levels rarely speak to one another.

Molecular and imaging findings do not fully describe the brain models and interfaces that are built, while the brain models rarely return molecular measures or interpretable cognitive or subjective experience levels.

Moreover, molecular mechanisms seldom constrain how imaging of human subjective experience and cognition is interpreted, while it remains an ongoing debate about whether AI-based simulations can generate subjective experience.
Clinically, this lack of integration produces an uneven field.

For instance, Alzheimer's disease research and diagnostics is increasingly supported by biomarkers [7], while in mental disorders -although reconceptualized as brain-based, robust biomarkers remain scarce and diagnoses remain largely based on verbal reports [8] [9] [10].

text.text: The central argument we propose is that the gap is not primarily due to technological limitations but about integration: molecular precision, human neuroimaging and AI models have each advanced along separate trajectories, with separate communities and standards, so that what one field establishes rarely becomes a basis or constraint on what the next field assumes.
In this Perspective we examine three rapidly moving domains in neuroscience and argue for the need for integration across research traditions, measurement scales and strategies.

These domains are: (1) molecular and cellular neuroimaging and neurotechnology, including recent progress in engineered ion channels, molecular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or ultrasound imaging, which supply unprecedented mechanistic detail that higher-level models otherwise merely assume; (2) human neuroimaging, combined with computational and translational strategies, which has begun to deliver comprehensive predictive whole-brain models of mental processes in humans and to translate these into novel brain models and treatment evaluation and may as such have the potential to integrate neuroscience and brain modelling across scales; and (3) datadriven and AI-inspired brain modelling, including whole-brain simulation, digital twin brains, and recent developments in BCIs, which can overcome recent constraints and allow generative brain models and interventions.

These three approaches require an integrative framework, and while precise measurement and simulations are essential, models that lack mechanistic and biological grounding may predict accurately but without explaining how neural systems give rise to cognition and behavior, or offering translational value for brain-based disorders.
To close this gap, in this work we review recent progress in each domain and in turn consider how these advances may collectively enable further progress.

We argue that the decisive advance will not come from further gains within any single layer, but from frameworks and approaches in which molecular, human and computational evidence constrain and support one another well enough.
We close with a roadmap of the key questions and translational milestones needed to facilitate this progress.

Understanding brain function requires detailed knowledge of its physiological and pathological processes at the molecular level, as a foundation for interpreting their consequences on connectivity, cognition, and behavior.

Modern advances in neurotechnology now provide unprecedented access to these processes, enabling direct investigation of complex molecular systems, such as ion channels that govern neuronal signaling, as well as the development of molecular imaging techniques capable of capturing activity across multiple spatiotemporal scales.
These complementary approaches span molecular and synaptic, cellular, mesoscopic, and macroscopic levels of brain organization and function (Figure 1).

text.text: In this section, we briefly outline state-of-the-art approaches that generate these new insights, highlighting both their unique advantages and their current limitations.
The synapse is the fundamental structural and functional unit that connects neurons and forms precise neural circuits throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems.

Synaptic proteomics has revealed approximately 1,800 synapse-enriched proteins that define 18 distinct neuronal synapse subtypes [15], as well as diverse presynaptic neurotransmitter vesicles and postsynaptic neurotransmitter receptors (ion channels and G-protein-coupled receptors, in most cases).

text.text: However, our understanding of how synaptic proteins assemble in their native environments and whether distinct cell types or neural functions utilize specialized synaptic components, remains limited.
To achieve the next level of resolution in understanding synapse formation and function, at least three major questions need to be addressed.

First, how can presynaptic components, including neurotransmitter vesicles and their associated molecular partners, be selectively isolated and analyzed (e.g. by means of mass spectrometry) at cell-typespecific resolution?
Second, how can postsynaptic receptors be directly visualized and identified in vivo with cell-type-specific precision?
Third, how can differences in synaptic composition and properties be linked to specific neural circuit functions and behaviors?

For instance, a recent study demonstrated that sleep-dependent synapse loss is regulated by sleep pressure at the level of the single neuron in zebrafish, providing direct evidence that synapse-level properties can be causally tied to behavioral state [16].

text.text: Addressing these questions requires integrating emerging technologies that bridge molecular, circuit, and functional scales, which have substantially advanced in recent years.
To highlight this progress, we briefly review emerging methods that have provided crucial insights into the molecular assembly and function of synapses and their major components.

Following this, we then further augment the overview with the state-of-theart neuroimaging methods, which help expand this knowledge by providing information across different scales, i.e. from studying molecular-level processes, to their implications on behavior and mental states.

Modern progress in investigating the synapses starts with patch-seq, a combination of patchclamp electrophysiology with single-cell ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing [17], which enables direct correlation of electrical properties with transcriptomic profiles in individual neurons and thus linking ion channel function to a given cell-type identity.

On the other hand, neuroimaging is entering a new phase in which the central challenge is to connect biological processes across scales, while preserving biological specificity, temporal fidelity and quantitative interpretability.

At the cellular and subcellular scale, fluorescence imaging remains a cornerstone of fundamental neuroscience, with an expanding repertoire of genetically encoded sensors enabling cell-type-specific visualization of various metabolic, calcium-, voltage-, neurotransmitter-and neuromodulator-related processes, thus providing essential insights with high spatiotemporal resolution and molecular-level specificity, albeit over a limited field of view [24, 25].

text.text: Although the spatial and temporal resolution of MR-based methods remain lower than that of optical and ultrasound methods, their depth, coverage and translational potential make them indispensable for connecting mechanistic imaging in experimental models with human neuroscience and clinical research.
In brief, the future of neurotechnologies, including neuroimaging, demands integration, rather than competition among modalities.

Consequently, the most recent advances in this research field are moving toward a cross-scale framework in which molecules, cells, vessels, circuits and whole-brain networks are not treated as separate domains, but as interconnected levels of the same biological system.

Over the past three decades, methodological innovation in animal and human neuroimaging, together with parallel theoretical advances, has transformed our understanding of the neural bases of cognitive, affective and social processes and of their dysregulation in mental disorders, driving a reconceptualization of these conditions as brain-based disorders.
Population initiatives such as the UK Biobank have acquired imaging data from more than 100,000 individuals [45], and clinical consortia have pooled data for large-scale case-control studies.

text.text: Together, technological progress combined with cognitive, affective and computational neuroscience is moving the field from mapping emotions onto isolated brain regions toward precise, individualized and ecologically valid models of conscious experience, and from descriptive biomarkers toward markers that support diagnosis, drug development and neuromodulation.

Realizing this potential will require prospective validation, individual-level reliability and integration with the molecular mechanisms and generative brain models discussed in the adjacent sections.
Building integrative models of brain function requires linking molecular and cellular mechanisms to distributed neural activity and individual behavior.
Advances in electrophysiology, computational simulation, and AI provide complementary approaches to this problem.

Largescale recordings constrain the dynamics that models must explain; mechanistic simulations specify how biological interactions generate these dynamics; and AI models learn transferable representations and predictive relationships from heterogeneous data.
Their integration offers a path toward digital twin brains that capture individual characteristics and generate experimentally testable predictions.
Here, we consider progress across these approaches and the challenges of connecting measurement, simulation, and intervention.

The present review focused on three exemplary domains (which align with our expertise) to illustrate the current momentum of technology-driven progress in neuroscience.

At the same time the overview underscores the central problem outlined in the Introduction: each field has advanced rapidly along its own trajectory and excels where the others remain limited providing an opportunity for an integrated and more comprehensive perspective.

Molecular and cellular neurotechnology resolves synaptic composition, receptor organization and neurochemical signaling with exceptional specificity, but how these properties relate to complex behavioral regulation remains incompletely understood (for an exception, see e.g.
Suppermpool et al., 2024 [16]), in particular for complex mental processes in humans.

text.text: Human neuroimaging now decodes complex and highly subjective mental states with high accuracy, but despite progress in prediction these neurofunctional signatures remain largely uninformative about the underlying neural and molecular mechanisms.

Data-driven and AI-based brain models simulate, predict and increasingly generate brain dynamics, but their parameters are not necessarily biologically grounded, and different mechanisms may reproduce the same observations.

We propose that the next level of progress will require integrating these domains into a dynamic and multi-directional closed loop of reciprocal constraints: molecular measurements that inform or fix model parameters, human signatures that define what models must reproduce and generate, and model predictions that prioritize molecular and neural perturbations for experimental testing (Figure 3).

text.text: From the bottom up, molecular measurements and molecular-scale architectures can inform assumptions in higher-level models.

Whole-brain simulations have begun to incorporate macroscale estimates of brain architecture, for example from MRI [86], yet they do not specify architecture or action at the molecular and mechanistic level.

text.text: Technology-supported advances in molecular neuroscience, including cell-type-specific synaptic proteomics, in situ ultrastructure, and receptor-, metabolism-and neurotransmitter-sensitive molecular indices could in combination with the dedicated computational implementation progressively anchor and constrain model parameters in biology.

From the top down, human neuroscience can define the outcomes against which models are evaluated and thus ensure their relevance for behavior and mental processes, given that precision alone does not guarantee relevance for behavior or mental health [87] [88] [89].

text.text: Current models are primarily validated against intrinsic functional connectivity and task-evoked activation patterns, whereas complex cognitive processes or also dysregulated subjective experiences for which patients seek treatment, such as fear, pain, arousal or depressed mood, are not yet a model output, although they may be approximated by neurofunctional signatures (e.g. [90]).

text.text: Carefully validated and behaviorally relevant neurofunctional signatures of these mental states and from corresponding data use to train the model (e.g. fMRI or EEG data) could provide benchmark targets for models and digital twins to infer behavioral and cognitive relevance.

This would allow simulated perturbations to be evaluated against changes in distinguishable experiences rather than in brain dynamics alone, with predictions that can in turn be tested, for example, by pharmacological neuroimaging in humans or focused brain stimulation experiments.

Together these models can in turn close the loop and identify the circuit-level and neurochemical systems on which molecular approaches can focus to determine mechanisms that regulate behavior and cognition.

In addition, animal research on internal emotion models offers a route to -potentially -link these models to mechanisms that remain inaccessible in humans, provided that crossspecies paradigms capture comparable computations [52].

text.text: The loop closes through intervention, which links targeted manipulations to predicted outcomes -ultimately behavioral and mental processes -and provides a common experimental currency across domains and scales.

Sonogenetic cell-selective modulation, pharmacological crosschallenges, connectivity-guided brain stimulation and virtual perturbation of AI surrogate brains all converge on the same experimentally critical question of how a controlled intervention propagates through neural circuits and what changes it induces in the dynamic system at different levels in comparison to a well-defined control condition.
Initial studies have begun to crossvalidate model predictions with empirical data.

text.text: Processspecific neurofunctional signatures have been used to capture potentially treatment-relevant effects of oxytocin on naturalistic fear [66] and, in closed-loop decoded neurofeedback, to reduce amygdala responses to phobic stimuli in patients with specific phobia [91].

text.text: A fully integrated framework, ideally a bidirectional closed loop, would require that interventions predicted in silico are constrained and tested by molecular imaging in experimental models and by neural signatures and behavioral or experience-based outcomes in humans, with discrepancies used to rapidly adapt the models.
Realizing this loop requires addressing challenges that are shared across the three domains and cannot be solved within any single one.
First, prediction must be distinguished from explanation: decoders can track experience without revealing mechanism, and simulations can reproduce the same outcomes through multiple mechanisms.
Second, reliability and specificity at the level of the individual remain limited, although personalization of models and approaches may be key to translation into mental health applications.

Third, ecological validity, feasibility and scalability: findings acquired under controlled laboratory conditions need to translate into daily life and, ultimately, into improved diagnosis and treatment of individuals with brain-based disorders.
Finally, the growing weight of private investment makes shared standards and neuroethical governance an urgent rather than a future requirement.
While challenges remain within and across domains, integration across approaches and scales will be critical to advance our understanding of the brain and its disorders.

For mental disorders in particular, which are still diagnosed largely on the basis of verbal report and for which translation from animal models has been limited, integration offers the opportunity to design, test and rapidly evaluate novel candidate drugs and innovative treatments before costly clinical trials, and to enable individualized diagnosis and intervention that is planned in a digital twin, delivered with novel neurotechnology and evaluated against changes in symptoms and experience-specific markers.
Success will therefore be measured not only by decoding accuracy or simulation scale, but by whether integrated models improve diagnosis, treatment selection and outcomes for individuals.

Achieving a mechanistic explanation of behavior and mental processes, and its translation into mental and brain health, will require that molecular, human and AI-based neuroscience constrain and support one another.

Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies (BRAIN) Initiative, the China Brain Project, or their European and Japanese counterparts are now increasingly flanked by rapidly growing private investment in neurotechnology, e.g. brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and digital brain platforms.
Companies such as Neuralink and Synchron have attracted substantial private investment in recent years.

Very recently (in March 2026), the first products have begun to enter the market, as China's National Medical Products Administration authorized the NEO implant reported as the first invasive BCI medical device to receive market approval for routine clinical application outside clinical trials.
Neuroscience is therefore no longer only a basic scientific enterprise but it increasingly demonstrates a potential to address key global health issues and produce measurable real-life impact.
